Machine learning systemTechnical Field

The presently disclosed subject matter relates to machine learning systems, autonomous device controllers, machine learning methods, and computer readable media.

Background

Neural networks are a popular paradigm for approximating almost any kind of function. The fact that their highly flexible parametric form in combination with large amounts of data allows for accurate modeling of the underlying tasks often leads to the most advanced predictive performance. While predictive performance is of course an important aspect, in many safety critical applications such as automatic driving automobiles, one also desires accurate uncertainty estimates with respect to predictions.

Bayesian neural networks have attempted to give neural networks the ability to model uncertainty, they assume a priori distributions over network weights, and by inference they can represent their uncertainty in posterior distributions. However, for such complex models, a priori selection is quite difficult, as understanding the interaction of parameters with data is a significant task. As a result, a priori convenience and ease of handling for calculations is often employed. Furthermore, reasoning over the weights of neural networks can be a daunting task due to the high dimensionality and posterior complexity.

An alternative way that the aforementioned problems can be "bypassed" is to take a random process. They directly assume the distribution over functions (e.g. neural networks) without the necessity to take a priori distribution over global parameters such as neural network weights. The Gaussian Process (GP) is an example of a random process. Unfortunately, there are two limitations to the gaussian process. For example, the underlying model is not very flexible for high dimensional problems and the training and reasoning costs are quite high, as it scales to the size of the dataset to the power of three.

Disclosure of Invention

To solve these and other problems, a machine learning system as defined in the claims is proposed. The machine learning system is configured to map input data instances to outputs according to a system map.

In an embodiment, the output is derived from the second potential input vector in the second potential space by applying a third function to the second potential input vector. A second potential input vector may be determined for the input data instance from a second potential reference vector obtained for a plurality of reference data instances identified as parents of the input data instance. Identifying the parent reference data instance may be based on similarity between a first potential input vector obtained for the input data instance and a first potential reference vector obtained for the set of reference data instances.

Interestingly, the output is derived from a second potential vector in a second potential space. The input instance is not mapped directly to the second potential vector, instead it is constructed from the reference instance with which it is associated. The relationship may be determined using the first potential space. This indirect process has the advantage that the system is forced to learn the structure of the input distribution well.

Preferably, the various mappings are random, not deterministic. The mapping may be repeated and averaged to improve accuracy if desired. Various machine learning functions may be applied to the first, second, and third functions. However, neural networks have proven to perform particularly well.

The machine learning system may be used for control of a physical system. For example, the input data instance and the reference data instance may comprise sensor data, in particular images. The output may include an output tag, for example, the system map may be a classification task. Other applications are possible. For example, the system may be trained to predict variables that are difficult to directly measure, e.g., the output may include physical quantities of the physical system, such as temperature, pressure, etc.

Detailed Description

While the presently disclosed subject matter is susceptible of embodiment in many different forms, there is shown in the drawings and will herein be described in detail one or more specific embodiments with the understanding that the present disclosure is to be considered as an exemplification of the principles of the presently disclosed subject matter and is not intended to limit the presently disclosed subject matter to the specific embodiments illustrated and described.

Hereinafter, elements of the embodiments are described in operation for the sake of understanding. However, it will be clear that the respective elements are arranged to perform the functions described as being performed by them.

Furthermore, the presently disclosed subject matter is not limited to the embodiments, and the presently disclosed subject matter resides in each and every novel feature or combination of features described herein or in the mutually different dependent claims.

The predictive task frequently occurs in computer vision. For example, autonomous device control, e.g., for an autonomous car, depends on a decision based on reliable classification. One problem with predictions made by machine learning systems is that there is often little distinction between predictions for situations where the system is well trained and predictions for situations where the system is not well trained. Consider, for example, a neural network trained to classify a road sign. If the network presents new, previously unseen landmarks, the neural network will likely be confident and possibly correctly classified. However, if an image, such as an image of a cat, that is outside the distribution of images used for training is presented to the neural network, the known neural network tends to still confidently predict landmarks for that image. This is an undesirable behavior, and thus there is a need for a machine learning system that would gently fail when presented with such an image, which is referred to as an "out-of-distribution (outside of distribution)" o.o.d. image. For example, in an embodiment, for points outside of the data distribution, the predictions may fall back to or near some default value.

Other advantages include providing a priori knowledge to the model, e.g., specifying the likelihood of induced bias (inductive bias). For example, nearby instances may be considered more likely to be parents of a given instance. This is much more intuitive than specifying a priori distributions over global latent variables. The coding of the vicinity may depend on the particular type of input data. For example, for an image, a distance metric, such as an L2 metric, may be used. Other distance metrics may be included if the input data includes other suitable data. For example, in an embodiment, the input data includes sensor data of a plurality of sensors. For temperature, a temperature difference, for pressure, a pressure difference, etc. may be used. However, the temperature and pressure data may be scaled appropriately to account for the different scales they appear in the modeled system. The multiple distance measures may be combined into a single distance, for example by a possibly weighted sum of squares.

An additional advantage is that the model is forced to learn the dependency structure between data instances. Furthermore, such dependencies may be visualized. Such visualization allows for debugging of the model. Alternatively, embodiments may calculate and visualize these dependencies. If the clusters shown in the so-called G-graph (examples of which are shown in fig. 5) or a-graph (these graphs are explained further below) do not fit reality, the modeler can use this information to further control the machine learning system, for example by increasing or decreasing the number of reference points or by changing a priori knowledge. A further advantage is that in an embodiment, an appropriate bayesian model can be obtained, which is exchangeable and consistent under marginalization, for example. This allows probabilistic modeling and inference of potential information without having to specify a priori distributions over global potential variables.

A new machine learning system is provided that may be used to train and/or apply machine-learnable functions. In an embodiment, two different potential spaces are used, such as a multidimensional vector space. The elements in these spaces are referred to as a first potential vector and a second potential vector, respectively. Vectors may also be referred to as points in vector space. An output, such as a prediction or classification, is made based on the second potential vector. A special set of reference data instances, which may be extracted from the same distribution as the input data instances, are mapped into a second potential space, which are second potential reference vectors.

For training examples other than the reference example, or for unseen input data examples, an indirection scheme is used. Both the training data instance and the reference instance are mapped to a first potential space. Thus, the reference data instance corresponds to a vector in a first potential space, e.g., by a first function, and corresponds to a vector in a second potential space, e.g., by a second function.

In a first potential space, a reference point associated with the training input instance is selected, e.g., the reference point is similar to the training input instance. The points in the second potential space are then derived from the corresponding points in the second potential space, e.g. they may be averaged, possibly with a weighted average. Finally, an output is calculated from the determined point in the second potential space. Thus, the system calculates the output indirectly from the input by selecting the relevant so-called parent. This forces the system to develop a better understanding of the input distribution structure. This facilitates a better understanding of the distribution of inputs and a better ability to identify unseen inputs that are poorly reflected in the input data.

Note that one or more or all of the mappings may be random. Instead of deterministically determining the output, a probability distribution is determined from which the mapping result is then sampled. This may be done, for example, for any of a mapping from the input instance to the first potential space, for a mapping from the reference instance to the second potential space, for determining a mapping of the parent, and for a mapping from the second potential space to the output.

This is indicated in fig. 3a by the dashed line from tag 324 to function 340, and in fig. 4 by the dashed line from tag 426 to potential space 436. This variant is possible because two potential spaces are used. For unknown inputs, only a mapping to the first potential space is required, and thus the second potential space may use labels in the mapping. Having the tag as an input in the second potential space increases the predictive power of the second potential space.

To include the tag 426 when mapped to the second potential vector, one may use a machine-learnable function, such as a neural network, that takes as input both the reference data instance and the tag. In a variant, two machine-learnable functions are used, for example two neural networks. The first machine-learnable function may map the reference data instance to the second potential space and the second machine-learnable function may map the tag to the second potential space, so that, possibly with weighting applied, the two second potential vectors may be added or averaged. The weighting factors may be learnable parameters.

Another variation that may be used with or in place of the previous variation is to provide the first potential vector of points 452 as a further input to the third function 370. This option is illustrated in fig. 3a as a dotted line from the first function 330 to the third function 370. It was found that adding this additional vector increases the extrapolation capability of the system. On the other hand, without this additional vector, the system more strongly resumes low confidence predictions when equipped with an o.o.d. input. Both may be preferred as appropriate.

An advantage of an embodiment is that the system reverts to or near the default output when facing the o.o.d. input. For example, given an o.o.d. input, the input may not have a parent and is therefore mapped onto a default vector in the second potential space. The latter is then mapped to or close to the default output. How close the measured output will be to the default output can be used to determine the confidence in the output.

For example, in an embodiment, the output of unit 370 may include a plurality of output probabilities for a plurality of tags. For example, if the input is a landmark, the output of the unit 370 may be a vector indicating a probability for each possible landmark that may be identified by the system. If a particular output is confidently identified, such as a particular landmark, one probability will be high and the remaining probabilities low, such as near zero. If no particular output is confidently identified, many or all probabilities will be approximately equal. Thus, confidence in the output can be derived by measuring how close the output is to the coincidence-closer to coincidence, less confident, and farther from coincidence, more confident. The confidence that the system has in its output can be reflected in a variety of ways, one way to do this is to calculate the entropy of the generation probability.

In an embodiment, the confidence value may be derived from the unit 370 that does not use the first potential vector as input. The confidence value indicates how well the input is represented among the training inputs. However, the output itself may be taken from the unit 370 using the first potential vector as input, so that the output has a better extrapolation.
